title: Long Island
description: Populous island in southeastern New York State
wiki_lead:
Long Island is a densely populated island in southeastern New York State, extending eastward into the Atlantic Ocean. Geographically, Long Island comprises four counties: Kings (Brooklyn), Queens, Nassau, and Suffolk. Kings and Queens counties form the western portion of the island and are boroughs of New York City, while Nassau and Suffolk counties occupy the central and eastern portions respectively.
Long Island extends about 120 miles (190 km) from New York Harbor eastward into the Atlantic Ocean and reaches a maximum width of about 23 miles (37 km). It has a total area of approximately 1,400 square miles (3,600 km2). The island was shaped largely by glacial processes during the Pleistocene, including the formation of terminal moraines and outwash plains.
In common usage, the term Long Island often refers specifically to Nassau and Suffolk counties, excluding Brooklyn and Queens because they are part of New York City; geographically, however, Brooklyn and Queens are located on the island.
Long Island is separated from Manhattan Island and the Bronx by the East River tidal estuary in the western part of the island. North of the island is Long Island Sound, across which lie Westchester County, New York, and the state of Connecticut. Across the Block Island Sound to the northeast is the state of Rhode Island. Block Island, which is part of Rhode Island, and numerous smaller islands extend farther into the Atlantic Ocean. To the southwest, Long Island, at Brooklyn, is separated from Staten Island and the state of New Jersey by Upper New York Bay, The Narrows, and Lower New York Bay.
Long Island's southern coast is bordered by a series of barrier beaches and islands separated from the main island by bays and lagoons. Fire Island is the longest of the barrier islands along the south shore and is separated from Long Island by Great South Bay. Other barrier beaches include those associated with Jones Beach Island and Long Beach Barrier Island.
As of July 1, 2025, the four counties comprising Long Island had an estimated combined population of 7,957,174. Kings County had an estimated population of 2,653,963; Queens County, 2,358,182; Nassau County, 1,398,939; and Suffolk County, 1,546,090. The 2020 United States census counted 8,063,232 residents across the four counties.
Long Island is the most populous island in any U.S. state or territory and one of the most populous islands in the world. Its population is concentrated heavily in the western portion, particularly in Brooklyn and Queens, while population density decreases toward eastern Suffolk County. Western Long Island is highly urbanized, while eastern Long Island contains suburban, agricultural, and undeveloped areas.
Long Island is culturally and ethnically diverse, encompassing densely populated urban neighborhoods, suburban communities, agricultural areas, and coastal communities. Housing costs and the availability of housing have been significant issues in Nassau and Suffolk counties as well as in New York City's Long Island boroughs.
As of 2024, Kings, Queens, Nassau, and Suffolk counties collectively had a gross domestic product of approximately US$558 billion. Economic activity on Long Island includes health care, education, professional and technical services, finance, manufacturing, retail, construction, transportation, and biotechnology. Biotechnology and scientific research play a significant role in the regional economy, with major research and educational institutions including Brookhaven National Laboratory, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, Stony Brook University, New York Institute of Technology, the Zucker School of Medicine, and the Feinstein Institutes for Medical Research.
The New York metropolitan area is served by several major airports located on Long Island. John F. Kennedy International Airport and LaGuardia Airport are located in Queens, while Long Island MacArthur Airport is located in Suffolk County. The region is also served by major air traffic control facilities, including New York TRACON and New York ARTCC.
Long Island has numerous bridges and tunnels connecting its communities with New York City's other boroughs and with the mainland. Ferries connect communities in Suffolk County with locations across Long Island Sound, including Connecticut, and with other points around the region.
The Long Island Rail Road (LIRR) is the largest and busiest commuter railroad in the United States and the oldest continuously operating commuter railroad in North America. The railroad operates 11 branches and serves more than 120 stations, connecting communities across Long Island with Penn Station and Grand Central Madison in Manhattan.
The Nassau–Suffolk labor market, which covers Nassau and Suffolk counties, had an unemployment rate of 4.0% in August 2026.

grok_lead: Long Island is a continental island and glaciated plain in southeastern New York, extending approximately 118 miles eastward from New York Harbor into the Atlantic Ocean, bounded by Long Island Sound to the north, the East River and New York Bay to the west, and the Atlantic Ocean to the south and east. It encompasses four countiesâKings (Brooklyn), Queens, Nassau, and Suffolk âcovering a land area of 1,401 square miles, with its widest point reaching 23 miles. As of 2023 estimates, the population totals over 7.8 million residents across these counties, accounting for more than 40% of New York State's populace and rendering it one of the most densely populated non-insular landmasses in the contiguous United States. The island's western end, integrated as the New York City boroughs of Brooklyn and Queens, features dense urban development intertwined with the metropolitan core, while the eastern expanse in Nassau and Suffolk counties transitions to affluent suburbs, agricultural zones like the North Fork vineyards, and coastal hamlets with beaches and maritime economies. Economically, Long Island drives regional prosperity through sectors such as healthcare, education, professional services, finance, and advanced manufacturing, with Nassau and Suffolk counties alone sustaining a GDP exceeding $200 billion annually and median household incomes surpassing $100,000, supported by low unemployment and a skilled workforce. These counties rank among New York State's most productive, bolstered by institutions like Stony Brook University and major employers in biotechnology and defense, though the full island's output, including urban contributions from Brooklyn and Queens, amplifies its national significance. Historically shaped by Algonquian indigenous groups, Dutch and English colonization, and post-World War II suburban boom facilitated by figures like Robert Moses through expansive parkways and public works, Long Island hosts pivotal infrastructure including John F. Kennedy International Airport and LaGuardia Airport, which handle substantial global air traffic. Notable landmarks encompass the Montauk Point Lighthouse, the Gold Coast estates emblematic of early 20th-century opulence, and natural features like the Pine Barrens, underscoring a blend of recreational, scientific, and cultural assets. Defining characteristics include environmental challenges from groundwater dependency and past industrial contamination, alongside debates over overdevelopment, high property taxes, and infrastructure strain amid population pressures.
